subtitle: Tell a true deadline from a habit of urgency, look past output to outcomes, and protect the quality of decisions that affect people's lives when the pressure is on.
audience: For staff who lead work, supervisors and team leads in DHS and DSD. It supports judgment about pace and priorities; legal deadlines, eligibility rules and formal decisions stay with the responsible office.

lessons.title: True deadlines and habits of urgency
objectives: Distinguish a true deadline, set by law, a person's need or a real consequence, from a habit of urgency.
Ask one question that shows whether a deadline is fixed.
Explain how a constant sense of urgency can crowd out checking, consulting and thinking.
Use Tema Okun's description of a sense of urgency as a lens on habits, not a label for people.
lessons.teaching:
Public service runs on deadlines, and many of them are real. A statute sets a date. A family needs a decision before a lease ends. A hearing is scheduled. Missing those dates causes harm, and meeting them is part of the work.

Other deadlines are habits. A request arrives marked urgent because everything on the team is marked urgent. A same-day turnaround becomes the norm because it happened once. Tema Okun's widely used list of organizational habits names a constant sense of urgency as one pattern that can make it hard to take time to be inclusive, think long-term or consider consequences. Okun offers the list as a tool for reflection. Use it here to look at habits, not to judge the person who sent the request.

One question often shows the difference: "What happens if this goes out tomorrow morning instead of today?" If the answer is "a family misses a deadline," the date is real. If the answer is "nothing, I just wanted it off my list," there may be time to check the work first.

Urgency has a cost even when the work gets done. Under time pressure, people use quicker rules of thumb. Research by John Payne, James Bettman and Eric Johnson found that people adapt their decision strategies to the time available, often by looking at fewer factors. That can work well for simple choices. For decisions that affect people's lives, the factor left out may be the one that mattered.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask what happens if it goes out tomorrow. A true deadline has a real consequence; a habit of urgency usually does not.
lessons.example: Practice case: At 4 p.m., the supervisor gets a request to send updated guidance to all case managers by the end of the day. The guidance changes how a form is filled out, and the supervisor has not had time to read it closely.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor do first?
choices: Send it out as is to meet the deadline.
Ask the sender what happens if it goes out at 10 a.m. tomorrow.
Stay late to rewrite it fully before sending.
feedback: The deadline is met, and nobody checked whether it had to be today or whether the guidance is clear.
One question shows whether the deadline is fixed, and buys time to check the guidance if it is not.
Dedicated, and it may not be needed. Pace set this way is hard to sustain and teaches the team that every request is an emergency.
lessons.reflection: Think about last week's urgent requests. How many had a real consequence if they waited a day?
lessons.action: For one week, sort each urgent request you receive into true deadline or habit of urgency, using the one-question test. Notice the pattern without naming anyone.

check.question: Which situation is a true deadline?
check.correct: A notice must be mailed by a date set in statute so a family keeps its appeal rights.
wrong: A manager wants a summary today because it was requested at the morning meeting.
A report is always sent on Fridays because that is how the team has done it.
check.feedback: A true deadline has a real consequence, such as a legal requirement or a person's rights. Preferences and routines can be valuable, and they can usually move when quality is at stake.

lessons.title: Output and outcomes
objectives: Distinguish output, such as cases closed, from outcomes, such as families who got what they needed.
Explain how counting only output can reward speed over quality.
Pair a count with an outcome question.
Recognize staff in ways tied to outcomes, not only volume.
lessons.teaching:
Output is what a team produces: cases closed, notices sent, calls answered. Outcomes are what changes for people: a family keeps its coverage, a person gets the right service, a problem stays solved. Both matter. Output is easier to count, so it often gets the attention.

Counting only output can quietly reward the wrong thing. Okun's list names "quantity over quality" as another common habit, where things that can be measured are valued more than things that cannot, such as the quality of relationships or a sense of fairness. If closing cases fast is all that gets noticed, people learn to close fast, even when a case is not really resolved.

A simple practice helps: pair every count with an outcome question. Four hundred cases closed is a number. How many of those families came back within 30 days is an outcome. The second question does not cancel the first. It tells you whether closing fast meant closing well.

Recognition shapes behavior. "Great work, everyone" is kind. "Great work, and fewer families had to come back this month" teaches the team what good work looks like.
lessons.keyPoint: Pair every count with an outcome question. Closing fast is only good if it means closing well.
lessons.example: Practice case: The division's monthly report shows 400 cases closed, a record. The program manager is preparing remarks for the team meeting.
lessons.question: What should the program manager ask?
choices: "How many of those families came back within 30 days?"
feedback: It rewards the count, and the count may already be hiding a problem.
This pairs the count with an outcome and shows whether closing fast meant closing well.
Recognition matters, and it is stronger when it is tied to outcomes the team can learn from.
lessons.reflection: What does your team count most often? What outcome would tell you whether that count means good work?
lessons.action: Choose one number your team reports. Write one outcome question to pair with it, and bring it to your next team meeting.

check.question: Which pair best shows output and outcome?
check.correct: Cases closed this month, and the share of families who returned within 30 days.
wrong: Cases closed this month, and cases closed last month.
Calls answered, and average call length.
check.feedback: An outcome shows what changed for people. Comparing one output with another output can show speed, but not whether people were well served.

lessons.title: A pause routine before decisions that affect people
objectives: Use a short pause routine before a decision that affects a client or community.
Ask who is affected and who has not been heard.
Use a premortem to surface risks before a plan is final.
Keep a pause short enough that it fits inside a real deadline.
lessons.teaching:
A pause does not have to be long to be useful. Before a decision that affects a client or a community, three questions take a few minutes: Who is affected by this? Who have we not heard from? What would we check if we had one more hour?

The second question often matters most. Notices that only go out in English, forms that assume a computer, meetings scheduled during work hours for people paid by the hour: these are common gaps that a rushed decision misses. Asking who has not been heard brings them into view while there is still time to act.

Gary Klein's premortem is another quick tool. Before a plan is final, the team imagines it is a few months later and the plan has failed. Each person writes down why. Klein describes this as a way to make it safe for people with doubts to speak, because the exercise asks for problems instead of treating them as disloyalty.

A pause routine fits inside a real deadline. It is not a reason to miss one. Ten minutes on the three questions, or twenty on a premortem, is often all a decision needs to catch the problem that would have cost a family weeks.
lessons.keyPoint: Before a decision that affects people, ask: Who is affected? Who have we not heard from? What would we check with one more hour?
lessons.example: Practice case: Near the end of the day, the case manager is about to close a case because a required form was not returned. A colleague mentions that the household's preferred language is not English, and the reminder letter was sent in English only.
lessons.question: What should the case manager do?
choices: Close the case, since the rules are clear and the form was not returned.
Pause, check whether the reminder reached the household in a language they read, and follow the agency's language access steps before deciding.
Keep the case open indefinitely to be safe.
feedback: The rule may be clear, and the decision may rest on a notice the household could not read. The pause question "who have we not heard from" applies here.
This takes a few minutes, follows the required steps and protects both the household and the decision. It is the strongest choice.
Leaving a case open without a plan creates a different problem. The aim is a sound decision, not an indefinite delay.
lessons.reflection: Think of a recent decision your team made quickly. Who was affected, and who was not heard from?
lessons.action: Write the three pause questions on a card or in your notes. Use them before the next decision you make that affects a client or community.

check.question: What is the purpose of a premortem?
check.correct: To surface risks before a plan is final by imagining it has already failed and asking why.
wrong: To review what went wrong after a project has ended.
To delay a decision until everyone agrees.
check.feedback: A premortem looks ahead. Imagining failure makes it easier for people to name doubts while there is still time to change the plan.

lessons.title: When the deadline cannot move
objectives: Name a gap honestly when a fixed deadline arrives before the work is complete.
Tell partners what is late and when it will be ready.
Plan a follow-up so a gap closes instead of being forgotten.
Avoid creating a new risk by breaking a legal requirement.
lessons.teaching:
Some deadlines cannot move. A launch date set by law, a federal reporting date, a court order. When the work will not be fully ready, the choice is not between perfect and late. It is between hiding the gap and naming it.

Naming the gap means telling the people who rely on the work what is missing and when it will be ready. If translated notices are late, county partners and community organizations can help families in the meantime, but only if they know. A gap that is named can be managed. A gap that is hidden lands on the people least able to absorb it.

Set a date for closing the gap and put it where the team will see it. Urgent work has a way of crowding out the follow-up. A short list of "what we launched without" keeps it visible.

Afterward, ask what would have made the gap smaller. Was translation started late because it was scheduled last? Did the team learn about the date late? These questions improve the next launch more than working harder on this one.
lessons.keyPoint: When the deadline cannot move, name the gap, tell partners when it will be ready and track the follow-up.
lessons.example: Practice case: The program manager's division must launch a new eligibility process on a date set by law. Notices in Somali and Hmong will not be ready for two more weeks. The county partner asks how families who read those languages will learn about the change.
lessons.question: What should the program manager do?
choices: Launch and say nothing about the gap.
Launch, tell county partners which languages are late, share interim support and set a date for the rest.
Delay the launch until every translation is ready.
feedback: Families who cannot read the notice will not know what they missed, and partners cannot help.
The legal date is met and the gap is named, so partners can help families in the meantime. This is the strongest choice.
This breaks a legal requirement and creates a new risk for everyone, including families who were ready.
lessons.reflection: When has your team met a deadline by leaving something out? Did anyone outside the team know?
lessons.action: For your next deadline, keep a short list of anything that will launch late, who needs to know and the date it will be done.

check.question: A fixed legal deadline arrives before translated notices are ready. What is the best approach?
check.correct: Meet the deadline, tell partners which languages are late and when they will be ready, and track the follow-up.
wrong: Delay the launch until everything is ready.
Launch and fix the translations quietly later.
check.feedback: Naming the gap lets partners support families in the meantime. Quietly fixing it later leaves families unaware; delaying breaks the legal requirement.

cards.back: A date with a real consequence: set by law, by a person's need or by a scheduled decision.
Treating requests as urgent by default. Test it: what happens if it goes out tomorrow?
What a team produces, such as cases closed or notices sent.
What changes for people, such as families who keep coverage or do not need to return.
Who is affected? Who have we not heard from? What would we check with one more hour?
Imagine the plan has failed, then list why. It surfaces risks while there is still time to act.

sources.title: John W. Payne, James R. Bettman and Eric J. Johnson — Adaptive Strategy Selection in Decision Making (1988)
sources.note: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. Supports the finding that people shift decision strategies under time pressure, often by considering fewer factors.

sources.title: Tema Okun, White Supremacy Culture: Characteristics (updated 2025)
sources.note: Source for sense of urgency and quantity over quality as organizational habits. Okun describes the list as a tool for reflection and cautions against using it to accuse people; it is not an empirical diagnostic instrument.

sources.title: Gary Klein — Performing a Project Premortem, Harvard Business Review (2007)
sources.note: Describes the premortem: imagine a project has failed and list plausible reasons, making it safer for people with doubts to speak.

sources.title: U.S. Office of the Surgeon General — Framework for Workplace Mental Health and Well-Being
sources.note: Supports the link between sustainable work practices, autonomy over how work is done, and worker well-being.
